title: AI Governance and Responsible AI Leadership
objective: Can integrate the principles of responsible AI, organizational roles, and risk response into decision-making and governance.

sections.title: Governance is an ongoing system, not a one-time approval
paragraphs: AI governance is not a process that reviews whether to adopt AI only once. It is a system that connects the purpose, users, people affected, data used, anticipated errors, approvers, exceptions, monitoring, and reviews throughout the AI life cycle. The greater the potential impact of a use case, the more clearly it should define human oversight and pathways for appeals and correction.

The elements of responsible AI identified by AWS include fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, accuracy and robustness, governance, and transparency. Do not merely list these as checklist items; determine who may be affected and how, and what evidence will be used to verify the impact in this use case.

For example, if unexpected personal information is included in a response after an AI system for handling inquiries has been approved, record the conditions under which it occurred and its impact. Based on the audit results, the stakeholders reassess the risks and review the scope of use and approval conditions.

sources.label: Responsible AI: From Principles to Practice

sections.title: Define responsibility owners and escalation paths first
paragraphs: AI risks cannot be assessed by the technical team alone. Business owners define the intended uses and unacceptable outcomes, data owners verify the legality, quality, and usage conditions of the data, and risk, legal, and security personnel confirm control requirements. Front-line users must be able to report cases in which they experience errors or adverse impacts.

When assigning responsibilities, avoid the vague statement that “the AI team is responsible.” For each use case, decide who approves implementation, who performs routine monitoring, who can decide to suspend use, and who approves exceptions.

When unexpected bias, exposure of confidential information, dangerous recommendations, or regulatory concerns are identified, establish the sequence of reporting, assessing the scope of impact, restricting use, remediation, and reapproval. A reporting channel is also necessary so that users who discover problems can report them without fear of operational retaliation.

sources.label: Responsible AI: From Principles to Practice

sections.title: Verifying Fairness and Transparency in Context
paragraphs: Fairness is not the simplistic goal of always producing the same outcome rates for every group. In contexts such as hiring, lending, and healthcare, stakeholders confirm which disadvantages to which groups should be avoided, which errors have the greatest impact, and what data and legal or ethical constraints are applicable. Disadvantages caused by unrepresentative data or proxy variables are also investigated.

Explainability does not mean revealing every technical internal calculation. It means enabling affected people, business personnel, and auditors to understand that AI was used, the main factors behind the decision, its limitations, and how to request a recheck or submit an objection.

Record evaluation results together with the target groups, conditions, exceptions, and unresolved risks—not just convenient averages. When the data, use case, model, or regulations change, review the results instead of using the previous evaluation unchanged.

checkpoints.prompt: The business owner of a recruiting-support AI system is being asked to speed up the selection process. To deploy it in production while addressing potential harm to candidates and accountability, which approach is most appropriate to carry out continuously from before deployment onward?

choices.text: Prioritize processing speed and use the AI's recommendations as final decisions without human review.
choices.explanation: This eliminates human oversight, error correction, and channels for explanation in high-impact decisions.

choices.text: Check for bias only once at deployment and do not monitor the system afterward.
choices.explanation: Because the data, usage conditions, and regulations may change, audits and reviews after deployment are necessary.

choices.text: Limit problem reports to the AI team and do not accept feedback from candidates or operational staff.
choices.explanation: This eliminates channels for discovering and correcting problems reported by affected people and those using the system in the field.

choices.text: Evaluate affected groups and errors, and designate people responsible for approval, human oversight, audits, and reviews.
choices.explanation: In recruitment, assess before deployment which candidates could experience what kinds of harm. Assign the people responsible for approvals and human review, and continue auditing decision outcomes after deployment so that explanations and corrections can be provided when problems arise.

checkpoints.prompt: A municipal program owner has received a report that an AI providing guidance for benefits consultations included incorrect guidance in its response. After confirming the scope of impact and the controls in place, which action is the most appropriate to take first?

choices.text: Privately correct the error only for the user who reported it, and do not keep a record.
choices.explanation: You cannot identify other users who received the same error, its cause, or the basis for the correction.

choices.text: Record the incident, identify the responsible personnel and scope of use, apply the necessary usage restrictions, and proceed with correction, reevaluation, and reapproval.
choices.explanation: Correct. Treat the issue as control evidence and connect the impact assessment, interim response, and reassessment after the correction.

choices.text: Discontinue use of the AI indefinitely and do not investigate the cause or alternative methods.
choices.explanation: Use restrictions appropriate to the impact are necessary, but this skips the assessment of the cause, scope, and conditions for a safe recovery.

choices.text: Do not inform users that they are interacting with AI in order to prevent errors.
choices.explanation: Reducing transparency does not resolve the cause of the incorrect guidance or protect users.

checkpoints.prompt: The person responsible for planning a loan-advisory AI receives evaluation results showing that, although the overall average accuracy is high, inappropriate guidance is frequent for a particular user group. What is the most appropriate decision?

choices.text: Investigate group-specific errors, data representativeness, proxy variables, and business impact, then implement necessary mitigations and conduct a reevaluation.
choices.explanation: Correct. This connects fairness to the intended use and its impact, enabling evidence-based decisions about improvement and reapproval.

choices.text: Release the AI while ignoring group-specific results because the average accuracy is high.
choices.explanation: An average can conceal disadvantages affecting a specific group, making it impossible to assess fairness and risks related to the intended use.

choices.text: Delete records containing inappropriate guidance and report only the average accuracy to executives.
choices.explanation: This would destroy evidence of important risks and hinder appropriate governance decisions.

choices.text: Remove all attribute information from the evaluation data so that differences between groups are not considered.
choices.explanation: This would make it impossible to determine whether disadvantages exist and would merely avoid the evaluation that is needed.
